passage:
Shalini, you remember I moved to Edinburgh for my master's? The first winter nearly flattened me. By December it was dark by half past three. I'd wake up in the dark, walk to the lab in the dark and come home in the dark. I stopped answering your calls. I wasn't sad about anything in particular, just heavy and slow, like my batteries were running out. Then March came, the light came back, and so did I.
The second winter I was ready. I walked in the park every lunch hour, even in drizzle. I kept my wake time fixed. And when the heaviness began to drag again in November, I went to the university doctor and told her everything. She took it seriously and we made a plan. I'm Gargi, and this winter I actually answered your calls.

qa.q: What time was it dark by in December?
qa.a: It was dark by half past three.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel during the first winter?
qa.a: Gargi felt heavy and slow, as if batteries were running out, and withdrew from calls.

qa.q: What did Gargi do differently the second winter?
qa.a: Gargi walked in the park every lunch hour, kept a fixed wake time and saw the university doctor when the heaviness began.

qa.q: What might the first winter have been like for Shalini?
qa.a: Shalini may have felt worried or shut out when Gargi stopped answering calls.

grounding: A person's energy and mood dip in dark months and lift with the light, helped by time outdoors, routine and a doctor's support.

passage:
I share an office in Shimla with Elizabeth, and every winter I've seen the same change. In summer she's first in, humming, organising the tea fund. When the fog settles in December and the valley stays grey for weeks, she comes in late, eats lunch at her desk and stops humming. I don't know what goes on inside her; she never complains. This year I asked, gently, whether winters are hard for her. She paused, then said, "Every year. I didn't think anyone noticed." Now we take a short walk together at noon, when the sun sometimes breaks through. Last week she told me she'd booked a doctor's appointment, because this year felt heavier. In March, I expect the humming back.
Lavanya

qa.q: What does Elizabeth organise in summer?
qa.a: Elizabeth organises the tea fund.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel about the change in Elizabeth?
qa.a: Lavanya felt concerned, noticing the lateness and the lost humming every winter, and cared enough to ask gently.

qa.q: What steps are Elizabeth and Lavanya taking this winter?
qa.a: A short walk together at noon for daylight, and Elizabeth has booked a doctor's appointment because this year felt heavier.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth seem to feel when Lavanya asked about winters?
qa.a: Elizabeth seemed surprised and perhaps relieved, saying she didn't think anyone had noticed.

grounding: A colleague notices a person's energy and mood dip in grey months, and time outside plus a doctor's visit are the sensible steps.

passage: Gargi, beti, you think this winter heaviness is only yours? Sit with your Akash Chacha a minute. When I was twenty-five, working in Delhi, every December the fog came and swallowed the sun for weeks. I'd wake in the dark, go to office in the dark, come home in the dark. By January I could barely drag myself out of bed. Food tasted of nothing. I stopped calling friends. Then March would come and I'd feel alive again. One winter it got so heavy I couldn't work. My friend Rakesh took me to a doctor, who listened carefully and helped me. After that I made rules: a walk at lunchtime in whatever light there was, bed and waking at fixed times, and a Sunday call with friends. Winters stayed grey. But never that heavy again.

qa.q: Where was Akash working at twenty-five?
qa.a: In Delhi.

qa.q: How did young Akash feel by January?
qa.a: He felt heavy and low, barely able to get out of bed, with food tasting of nothing.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Akash's story?
qa.a: When the heaviness stopped him working, his friend Rakesh took him to a doctor, and he then built daily routines.

qa.q: How might Rakesh have felt seeing Akash that winter?
qa.a: Rakesh was probably worried and cared enough to take Akash to a doctor.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, low mood and energy in dark, foggy months that lift with brighter days, eased by getting outside, routines and a doctor.

passage: That winter in Shimla, the power went out almost every evening, and the sun barely cleared the hills before it sank again. Pooja, twenty-five, taught at a school on the ridge. By December she was exhausted all the time, craving sleep, and irritable with her students. She cried once in the staff room for no reason she could name. Her colleague Harsha noticed. 'You're not yourself. Is it the dark? I get it every year.' Harsha dragged her out for a walk in the noon sun every lunch break, even in the cold. Pooja kept her waking time fixed, even on Sundays. When the low mood still felt heavy after a month, she saw a doctor in town, who listened carefully and offered support. By February, as the days lengthened, Pooja felt her old energy returning.

qa.q: What went out almost every evening in Shimla?
qa.a: The power.

qa.q: How was Pooja feeling by December?
qa.a: She was exhausted, irritable and low, even crying without knowing why.

qa.q: What steps helped Pooja through the winter?
qa.a: Noon walks in the sun with Harsha, a fixed waking time and seeing a doctor when the low mood stayed heavy.

qa.q: How might Pooja's students have experienced her irritability?
qa.a: They may have felt confused or hurt by a usually kind teacher snapping at them.

grounding: Shows a young adult's energy and mood dipping in dark winter months, and getting outside, routines and a doctor's help as the sensible steps.

passage: The smog settled over Delhi in November, and with it came Joseph's familiar winter gloom. He woke tired, even after nine hours, and found himself dreading work he usually enjoyed. His wife, Parul, noticed he'd stopped playing his guitar in the evenings. 'You get like this every winter,' she said gently. 'And every spring you come back.' Joseph realised she was right. They made a plan together: breakfast on the balcony whenever there was light, a walk in Lodhi Garden at lunch, bed and wake times kept the same. Parul also suggested he see a doctor, since the low feeling had lasted weeks. The doctor listened and set up a follow-up. By mid-December, Joseph was still slower than in summer, but he picked up his guitar again.

qa.q: What had Joseph stopped doing in the evenings?
qa.a: Playing his guitar.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling as the smog settled in November?
qa.a: He felt tired and gloomy, dreading work he usually enjoyed.

qa.q: What sensible steps did Joseph take?
qa.a: Morning light on the balcony, lunchtime walks, fixed sleep times and seeing a doctor for the lasting low mood.

qa.q: How might Parul have felt seeing Joseph pick up his guitar again?
qa.a: She was probably relieved and happy to see a sign of his usual self.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing mood and energy dip in gloomy months, and getting outside, keeping routines and seeing a doctor as sensible steps.

passage:
"You've had the lamp on since breakfast," Rafiq said, dropping his bag.
"It's four o'clock and it looks like midnight. I hate December here."
"Last December you said the same thing. And in April you were planning picnics."
Maria pulled the blanket higher. "So I'm just a sunny-weather person?"
"Maybe your body notices the dark. You've stopped your lunch walk, you sleep till nine..."
"Because it's grey and freezing."
"Tomorrow at one, when the sky's brightest, I'll come with you. Twenty minutes round the lake."
"And if I still feel like this in a month?"
"Then we book the doctor. Feeling this heavy for weeks is worth asking about."
She was quiet for a while. "Okay. One o'clock. Bring the good gloves."

qa.q: What time does Rafiq offer to walk with Maria?
qa.a: At one o'clock, when the sky is brightest, for twenty minutes round the lake.

qa.q: What does Maria's pulling the blanket higher suggest about her mood?
qa.a: She feels low and a bit defensive, stung by the idea that her mood depends on the weather.

qa.q: What sensible steps does the conversation settle on?
qa.a: Getting out at the brightest time of day, restarting the lunch walk, and seeing a doctor if the heavy mood lasts.

qa.q: How does Rafiq see Maria's December mood?
qa.a: Rafiq sees a pattern rather than a flaw, since he remembers the same dip last December and her brighter spirits in April.

grounding: Illustrates a person whose energy and mood dip in the dark months, with getting outside, keeping routines and seeing a doctor if the low lasts as sensible steps.
